 Driving straight, steering can get heavy and EPS warning lights can come on. Honda says software in 635,808 Pilot, MDX and TLX vehicles can do it. VIN checks open Nov. 11. 
 Advertising 
 November 10, 2026 - 4:42AM EST 
 By: Noah Washington 
 On a straight road, steering can get heavy and EPS warning lights can come on, according to Honda's Part 573 filing for NHTSA recall 26V721 (Honda's own recall numbers are KQB and TQA), which covers 635,808 Honda Pilot, Acura MDX and Acura TLX vehicles. NHTSA's Nov. 9 acknowledgement letter says VINs become searchable on NHTSA.gov on Nov. 11, and the filing schedules owner letters for on or about Dec. 14.
 Open the poll in its own page 
 One 2025 Honda Pilot owner told NHTSA in complaint ODI 11698387, filed Nov. 8, 2025, that "while traveling straight at 25-30 mph, power steering suddenly failed." NHTSA complaints are unverified owner accounts, and this one also lists AWD and other dash warnings, so it is not tied to this recall's fault. Honda's filing, which estimates that 100% of the 635,808 vehicles carry the software, describes a similar setting: driving straight, with steering effort that increases once assist is disabled.
 NHTSA recall 26V721, which Honda numbers KQB and TQA, covers three models, and the counts add up to 635,808:
 2023-2025 Honda Pilot: 383,110 vehicles, built Sept. 13, 2022 to Dec. 23, 2025.
 2022-2024 Acura MDX: 177,100 vehicles, built Dec. 10, 2020 to July 10, 2024.
 2021-2025 Acura TLX: 75,598 vehicles, built Aug. 11, 2020 to Aug. 18, 2025.
 The Pilot is the largest group, and it is the SUV that some buyers testing the Toyota Grand Highlander ended up in . The MDX is also an SUV, and the TLX is a sedan. Honda built the population from manufacturing records. For context only, Honda's filing for last year's separate 2025 Acura RDX steering recall (NHTSA 25V582, 17,334 vehicles) estimated 0.3% with defect; that recall also ended in failsafe mode and a loss of assist, from a different calibration error. The 2025 Acura MDX and the 2026 Honda Pilot are not in this recall's population.
 Honda says the software can divide by zero, and the assist shuts off when it does 
 The filing names Robert Bosch Automotive Steering LLC of Florence, Kentucky as the supplier and lists 42 power steering rack part numbers. It says the supplier "developed incorrect EPS software containing an error in the Driver Attention Monitor road-condition compensation calculation and an improperly configured response to the resulting internal error." Then it spells out the mechanism: the software "may perform a floating-point division with a zero denominator, triggering an internal error. The EPS software was incorrectly configured to respond to this error by disabling power steering assist."
 The zero is the trigger, and the filing counts the response to it as a second error. Honda confirmed in February 2026 that the issue "only occurs under certain operating conditions when the vehicle is driving straight."
 Here is what a driver would see, in Honda's words:
 “If the EPS system enters failsafe mode, power steering assist is disabled, and the EPS warning indicators illuminate in the instrument cluster. Without power assist, steering effort increases, which may reduce vehicle controllability, increasing the risk of a crash or injury.”
 The filing and NHTSA's record carry no park-outside or do-not-drive advisory, and the filing sets no interim owner notice date. Increased steering effort with an EPS warning indicator is the symptom the filing describes, so anyone who sees it should call a dealer rather than wait for the letter.
 A 2022 Acura MDX Type S, which is in the 2022-2024 MDX recall population. Photo: Acura 
 The first report arrived in November 2021, and returned parts showed nothing 
 The filing's chronology runs almost five years from first report to recall decision:
 Nov. 29, 2021: "Honda received the first report of the issue."
 Aug. 2023 to Aug. 2025: Honda received more reports and worked with the supplier, but "due to the deletion of error codes by the dealer or supplier, no issues were found with returned parts."
 Aug. 22, 2025: the supplier identified the failure through market-return analysis.
 Dec. 2025: Honda recreated the issue by analyzing dashcam footage and analysis results.
 Oct. 22, 2026: Honda determined that a safety defect existed and decided to conduct a recall.
 The filing reports the deleted error codes without saying how many were deleted or why. It also counts "146 warranty claims, one report of an injury, and no reports of a death" from May 22, 2022 to Oct. 22, 2026. Those 146 claims sit against 635,808 vehicles over four and a half years, and a claim count cannot be read as a failure rate. Every vehicle on the list has the software, and the filing says the failure needs specific conditions. Being on the list and losing assist are different events.
 A 2024 Acura TLX A-Spec. Photo: Acura 
 The fix is a free reprogramming, and the letter is the last thing to arrive 
 Registered owners will be contacted by mail and asked to visit an authorized Honda or Acura dealer, where "The dealer will reprogram the EPS control unit with improved software." NHTSA's Nov. 9 acknowledgement letter says the work is free of charge, lists Honda customer service at 1-866-784-1870 and its own Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236, and says NHTSA is still reviewing Honda's proposed owner letter. Dealer notification was scheduled for on or about Oct. 30 and owner letters for on or about Dec. 14, per the filing, which is 45 days after the scheduled dealer notice.
 A free repair settles the cost. In Toyota's Tundra engine recall , owners also asked what a truck is worth after the repair, a question the Honda filing does not answer.
 One question stays open. The filing says "The affected models are no longer in production," yet Honda sells a 2026 Pilot, and the filing does not say whether that model carries the corrected software.
 Owners can check a VIN on Nov. 11 without waiting for the Dec. 14 letter 
 From Nov. 11, NHTSA.gov will show whether a specific VIN has this recall unrepaired. If you own a 2023-2025 Pilot, 2022-2024 MDX or 2021-2025 TLX, tell us in the comments whether your steering effort ever increased while driving straight, plus the model year, the miles and what the dashboard showed. Honda owners already send us real-world numbers, like a 2024 Honda Ridgeline owner's 15 MPG over a 5,853-mile Airstream trip to Alaska . A recall list says who could be affected, and miles say what happened, as a Toyota Tundra driver who logged 7,000 Arctic miles without the engine failure behind a 43,566-truck recall showed. This time the number we want is the mileage when the steering effort increased.
 About The Author 
 Noah Washington is a young automotive journalist based in Atlanta, Georgia, covering sports cars, luxury vehicles, electric vehicles, and the ownership realities behind them. His reporting for Torque News connects engineering and design with what drivers experience, from towing and charging to reliability and the character that makes a car worth caring about.
 His work includes interviews with Jaguar F-TYPE designer Matt Beaven and former Lucid Gravity chief engineer Zach Walker , plus firsthand reviews of the Nissan Z Nismo and Mitsubishi Mirage G4 .
 A BMW E36 M3 owner and former Miata owner, Noah has written for TopSpeed, HotCars, and Cointelegraph. He is a member of the Southeast Region Automotive Media Association (SERAMA) and the International Motor Press Association (IMPA) . His favorite car remains the Fiat 500 Abarth.
